title: Transferability Envelope Constraint
description:
A single statement bounding where a workflow's results are valid: which `role` this fact plays (what the workflow was trained on vs. what its results are valid for vs. where it can technically run), which `dimension` it concerns (spatial, temporal, ecological, climatic, jurisdictional, grid-structure, ... — an open vocabulary), and the `value` itself.
Repeatable, and `id`-addressable: rules cite a constraint by `id` to say which boundary they are evaluated against, so a workflow with two different footprints can state which artifact each one governs. FP-WF1 needs three constraints at once (trained-on/spatial, valid-for/ecological, can-run-on/climatic), which is why role and dimension are independent axes rather than a single enum choice.
**Values bind to published vocabularies rather than to FOCAL terms wherever one exists**, so a consumer that already understands GeoSPARQL or DCAT can evaluate the constraint without knowing anything about FOCAL: a spatial extent is a `geo:Geometry` carrying `geo:asWKT`, a calendar span is a `dcterms:PeriodOfTime` carrying `dcat:startDate`/`dcat:endDate`. That is what makes "can I run this workflow over my area of interest?" a query a GeoSPARQL engine can answer with `geof:sfWithin`, rather than a sentence a person has to read.

id.description:
Identifier for this constraint, so a rule can cite it in `when[].constraint`. Optional only for a constraint no rule refers to.
An **IRI, a CURIE, or a bare local name** (see bblocks://ogc.ogc-utils.iri-or-curie). A local name is resolved against the document's base URI and is right for a constraint specific to one workflow. An IRI or CURIE gives the constraint a **global identity**, which is what makes a boundary shareable: the EURO-CORDEX EUR-11 domain is the same extent for several FOCAL workflows, and each restating it as a private local name leaves nothing able to tell that they are the same boundary. Declaring it here under its global identifier says so.
A CURIE expands only if its prefix is declared in the JSON-LD context (via `x-jsonld-prefixes` or an imported block); an undeclared prefix is read as a URI scheme and `acme:eur11` stays `acme:eur11`, which validates and means nothing. Use a full IRI unless the prefix is known to be in scope.
Giving a constraint a global identifier makes the boundary shareable, not fetchable: it is still declared in full in every statement that cites it, so a reader always has the extent in front of them. What the identifier buys is being able to ask which workflows are bounded by this exact domain.

role.description: Which aspect of the envelope this statement describes. Open vocabulary — see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab.

dimension.description: Which axis of variation this statement constrains, and therefore what shape `value` takes. Open vocabulary, seeded from the eight FOCAL pilot questionnaires and expected to grow; a new term needs no schema change unless it also needs a new `value` shape.

transferabilityNotes.description: Why this value is what it is, where that is not self-evident: an approximated geometry, a fact inferred rather than stated by the source, a granularity the source left open. Uplifts to `rdfs:comment`. Mixed in from bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.notes.

value.description:
The constraint value, shaped by `dimension`:
- `spatial`/`jurisdictional` — a geometry, as `{"asWKT": "POLYGON((...))"}`. WKT rather
  than GeoJSON coordinate arrays: it uplifts to a real `geo:wktLiteral`, which is the
  form GeoSPARQL's topological functions actually operate on, it is one value rather than
  a nested array so nothing is lost or reshaped in uplift, and it is dramatically more
  compact (UP-WF2's European coverage MultiPolygon costs a few hundred characters
  instead of 1,283 lines of Turtle). An approximate extent is expected and fine — a
  published bounding box for a model domain, say — but it must be a real extent, since a
  free-text place name cannot answer the containment question this dimension exists for.
- `temporal` — either `{"startDate", "endDate"}` (a calendar span, uplifting to
  `dcat:startDate`/`dcat:endDate` on a `dcterms:PeriodOfTime`) or `{"scenarioMarker"}`
  for results that are not calendar-indexed at all. A Global Warming Level is the
  evidenced case: it is reached in different years under different emissions scenarios
  and ensemble members, so a calendar interval would be a fabrication rather than a
  simplification. Markers are concepts, not free text, so `GWL+1.5` written two ways by
  two pilots is one thing rather than two.
- `grid-structure` — the set of grid types the workflow's gridded inputs may be on, as
  `{"gridTypes": ["regular-latlon", "rotated-pole"]}`. A whitelist rather than a
  description: `inside` means the target data's grid is one of these, `outside` that it
  is not. This is a structured branch and not prose because UP-WF3's constraint ("other
  projections are not handled") is a hard interface requirement over a small enumerable
  set — mechanically checkable, and *more* so than a bounding box, since the terms carry
  the CF-conventions `grid_mapping_name` as their `skos:notation` and the datasets in
  question declare exactly that.
- **any dimension, as an analogy** — `{"scheme": ..., "sameClassAs": ...}`, saying the
  target must fall in the same class of a published classification as some reference
  does. This is the shape of every "comparable to where we calibrated" claim in the
  corpus, and it is a *relation*, not a value: the source says the target must resemble
  the training area, and says nothing about which classes the training area is in.
  Enumerating those classes would state something the source never said and would go
  stale the moment the training geometry is corrected, so the default is to name the
  reference and let a platform derive the rest. Tested with `same-class-as` /
  `different-class-from` rather than `inside`/`outside`.
- `ecological`/`climatic`/anything else — a plain string, where no classification
  captures the claim. "A comparable ecological range" does not become machine-checkable
  by being wrapped in coordinates it does not have. A rule may still cite such a
  constraint; the condition is then a judgement a person makes, stated in the same
  structure, which is honest about where automation stops. Prefer the analogy shape above
  where a scheme does capture it: it says the same thing and a machine can settle it.

oneOf.title: Grid structure (set of accepted grid types)
Classification analogy (any dimension)
oneOf.description: Available on every dimension, including spatial ones: "the same biogeographical region as the training area" is a different claim from "inside the training area's bounding box", and both are legitimate.

asWKT.description: The extent as a WKT literal, uplifting to `geo:asWKT` with datatype `geo:wktLiteral`. An optional leading CRS URI is permitted, per GeoSPARQL; without one, CRS84 (longitude/latitude in degrees) is assumed, as GeoSPARQL specifies.

startDate.description: Start of the period, as an ISO 8601 year, year-month, or date. Granularity is workflow-specific and deliberately not fixed, but the format is, so two periods stated at the same granularity compare correctly as plain string ordering.

endDate.description: End of the period, in the same form as `startDate`.

gridTypes.description: The grid types the workflow accepts, as concepts from the FOCAL grid-types scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). The whole array is the constraint: a target is `inside` it if its grid is one of these. Open vocabulary, seeded only with the two terms UP-WF3 evidences and cross-walked to CF-conventions `grid_mapping_name` values, so adding a projection is a lookup in the CF table rather than a judgement.

scheme.description: The published classification system this constraint is evaluated in, as a concept from the FOCAL classification-schemes vocabulary (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). FOCAL names the scheme and records where its terms live; it does not restate them, the same discipline applied to QUDT units and CF grid mappings.

sameClassAs.description: The reference whose classification the target must share, normally the `id` of another constraint in the same envelope — typically the `trained-on` extent. **This is the preferred form**, and the only one usable with a scheme that publishes no term identifiers: nothing has to name a class, so a platform classifies the reference geometry and the target and compares. It also stays correct when the reference geometry is replaced by a better one, which an enumerated class list would not.

classes.description: Explicitly stated classes, as an alternative to naming a reference. Use only where the source actually states them: deriving them from a reference and writing them here turns an inference into an assertion. Cite the scheme's own identifiers — EUNIS habitats are published by the EEA, and Koppen-Geiger classes are published by FOCAL itself (`.../koppen-geiger/Cfb`) precisely because no maintainer publishes them. Each classification-schemes concept records where its terms live.

scenarioMarker.description: A non-calendar, scenario-indexed temporal position, as a concept from the FOCAL scenario-markers scheme (see bblocks://ogc.focal.transferability.vocab). Open: other scenario indices may follow.
